title: Not things, but judgments
hook: people are upset not by things but by their judgments about things (Enchiridion 5)
tomorrow: The horse is handsome, not you

segments.voice: Yesterday: Epictetus, going to the baths. Your line was and keep my purpose. Did you add those words before walking through a door? Day three hundred thirty-seven.

Two people are stuck in the same traffic jam, same lane, same minute. One is pounding the wheel, already rehearsing the apology to the boss. The other has turned up the radio and is singing badly. Same cars. Same delay. Same red brake lights stretching to the bridge. So what, exactly, is upsetting the first driver? If it were the traffic, it would be upsetting both of them. Section five of the handbook gives Epictetus' answer, and it fits in a single breath. Today: not things, but judgments.
screen: `TWO DRIVERS, ONE JAM.` → `ONE FURIOUS, ONE SINGING.` → `WHAT'S DOING THE UPSETTING?`

segments.voice: First, the sentence. In George Long's translation: "Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things." The Greek word for those opinions is dogmata, the plural of today's word. Second, the word. We hear dogma and think of rigid doctrine, something you're not allowed to question. In Epictetus' Greek it's humbler. It comes from a verb meaning to seem. A dogma is what seems so to you: your view, your verdict, the judgment you've already passed before you notice you passed it. The traffic is a thing. I'm going to be fired, this always happens to me: those are dogmata. Third, his example. Death, he says, isn't terrible, or it would have seemed so to Socrates, who faced his own calmly. The terrible part is the judgment that death is terrible. You can disagree with him about death and still try the move on a parking ticket. Then he adds a ladder. An untrained person blames others when things go badly. Someone starting out blames themself. Someone trained blames neither. Fourth, the long echo. The novelist Laurence Sterne put this sentence, in Greek, at the front of Tristram Shandy. And in the twentieth century the psychologist Albert Ellis named Epictetus as an influence on his therapy, which taught people to catch the belief that sits between an event and the feeling. Here is the honest limit. Epictetus isn't saying pain is imaginary or that nothing out there is wrong. He's saying the part that churns inside is built partly from our own verdicts. And a verdict can be looked at again.
screen: `NOT THE THINGS, BUT THE OPINIONS.` · `DOGMA: WHAT SEEMS SO TO ME.` · `SOCRATES, AND THE LADDER OF BLAME.` · `FROM STERNE TO THE THERAPY ROOM.` · then, large: `IT'S MY VIEW.`

segments.voice: Bring back one thing that upset you this week. Something small is fine: a text, a delay, a look. First, describe only what happened, the way a camera would see it. He replied with one word. The train came twelve minutes late. Then find the judgment underneath. He's annoyed with me. My whole day is ruined. Say it plainly, and then add: it's my view. Don't argue with it yet. Just see that it's a view, sitting there. The bell holds the time.
Dogma. In Epictetus' Greek, not rigid doctrine but a judgment, what seems so to you. It's our dogmata, he says, that disturb us. Today's word.
Your line: it's my view. The next time something stings today, split it in two: what happened, and what I'm saying about it. Day three hundred thirty-seven.

screen: `DAY 337 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE HORSE IS HANDSOME, NOT YOU.`

howItsDone: People who practice Stoicism often separate what happened from the judgment they've added to it, sometimes writing the two side by side.

myth: in Epictetus' Greek, dogma means a rigid doctrine you can't question
it means a judgment or opinion, what seems so to you.
Laurence Sterne put this line in Greek at the front of Tristram Shandy
the handbook's fifth section opens the novel.
he says our judgments about things are what disturb us, not that nothing happens.

fork.setup: your project went badly. on Epictetus' ladder, what does someone fully trained do?
fork.reveal: the untrained blame others, beginners blame themselves, the trained blame neither and look at their judgments.

original.note: Greek, Enchiridion 5: a judgment, an opinion; from a verb meaning to seem.

trapdoor: what you thought: dogma means stubborn doctrine.
what it means: a judgment, what seems so to you, and the thing Epictetus says actually disturbs us.
what a scholar hears: dogmata, from dokein, to seem; the line was Sterne's epigraph, and Albert Ellis cited Epictetus as a forerunner of his therapy.

δόγμα from δοκεῖν, 'to seem': standard (LSJ); confirm.
